title: Discovering state-of-the-art quantum circuits with large language models
authors: Andi Gu, Alek H. Kemeny, Susanne F. Yelin, Mikhail D. Lukin
abstract: Significant efforts are currently being directed toward the implementation of large-scale quantum information processors, but realizing useful quantum advantage also requires the development of efficient quantum algorithms. While for many practical problems the dominant resource costs are associated with a small set of computational primitives, optimizing them in the quantum setting presents unique challenges, including a reversibility constraint absent from ordinary classical computation. Here we introduce an evolutionary framework in which large language models (LLMs) propose circuit designs and an independent evaluator verifies and scores them. We apply this framework to tasks spanning numerical computation, chemistry, optimization, quantum simulation, and number theory. In seven of the eight tasks, the discovered circuits significantly reduce both Toffoli and qubit counts relative to the state of the art. In the eighth, the search discovers a new reversible architecture for prime-field modular inversion. By handling reversibility differently, the architecture makes divsteps -- a classical algorithm previously impractical for reversible integer arithmetic -- viable and substantially improves the Toffoli-qubit trade-off for modular inversion. These results open the door for evaluator-guided LLM co-design of new algorithmic structures for quantum computation.

infographic.key_insight: Evaluator-guided LLM search discovers quantum circuits that reduce both Toffoli and qubit counts in seven of eight tasks and a new modular-inversion architecture in the eighth.
infographic.engineering_relevance: More resource-efficient reversible primitives could lower quantum-computing costs across numerical computation, chemistry, optimization, simulation, and number theory.
method: Use LLMs to propose circuit designs in an evolutionary search.
Independently verify and score candidate circuits.
Explore new reversible architectures alongside circuit optimizations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across eight tasks, the abstract reports significant Toffoli and qubit reductions in seven and an improved Toffoli–qubit trade-off for prime-field modular inversion using divsteps in the eighth.
infographic.watch_item: Circuit resource reductions do not establish hardware-level speedups; the abstract does not report physical-device validation.
infographic.paper_title: Discovering state-of-the-art quantum circuits with large language models

title: Quantum-Classical Neural Networks for Solving Lindblad Master Equations
authors: Rafael Florencio Díaz, Julio Guerrero García, Elvira Romera Gutiérrez
abstract: Variational quantum algorithms have emerged as a promising approach for simulating open quantum systems, yet their expressive power and trainability remain poorly understood. We propose a variational framework for solving Lindblad master equations by minimizing a residual cost function using a compositional ansatz obtained by combining a classical neural network with a parameterized quantum circuit. The density matrix is represented through a purification on an enlarged Hilbert space, ensuring positivity, Hermiticity, and unit trace by construction, while all gradients are evaluated exactly via the parameter-shift rule. Beyond the algorithmic formulation, we derive an upper bound for the covering number of the proposed compositional model and compare it with that of purely quantum neural networks. Our analysis shows that the classical parametrization enlarges the effective hypothesis class while providing finer control over its complexity, thereby establishing a theoretical connection between expressivity, covering numbers, effective dimension, and the barren plateau phenomenon. Numerical experiments validate both the accuracy of the proposed method for representative Lindblad master equations and the theoretical predictions regarding gradient concentration. These results provide a unified variational and theoretical framework for the simulation of dissipative quantum dynamics using compositional quantum machine learning models.

infographic.key_insight: A classical neural network combined with a parameterized quantum circuit forms a variational model for Lindblad equations, with theoretical links between expressivity, model complexity, and gradient concentration.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework targets dissipative quantum-system simulation while preserving physically valid density matrices by construction.
method: Minimize a Lindblad-equation residual using a classical–quantum compositional ansatz.
Represent density matrices through purification to ensure positivity, Hermiticity, and unit trace.
Use parameter-shift gradients and covering-number bounds to analyze training and expressivity.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments on representative Lindblad equations support solution accuracy and theoretical predictions about gradient concentration; the abstract provides no quantitative benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Purification requires an enlarged Hilbert space, and the abstract does not establish scalability or robustness on noisy quantum hardware.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum-Classical Neural Networks for Solving Lindblad Master Equations

title: Demonstration of Logical Error Suppression in a Surface Code Memory on a Cloud-Accessible IBM Superconducting Processor
authors: Shuwen Kan, Aaron Hoyt, Sean Garner, Ethan Vo, Adrian Harkness, Rod Rofougaran
abstract: Quantum error correction can suppress logical errors exponentially with code distance when physical noise is below threshold. Realizing this on hardware requires tight coordination among quantum gates, mid-circuit measurements, and qubit coherence. Device variation, noise asymmetry, and correlations across space and time complicate the translation of these capabilities into logical error suppression. Here, we study rotated surface-code memory on an IBM Nighthawk r2 processor. Performance varies across tested processor placements, which we attribute to differences in qubit quality. We optimize the code by combining short readout, fused measurement and reset, and an XX echo on data qubits during ancilla readout. Compared with standard readout without reset or echo, the optimized syndrome extraction circuit reduces the median per-round logical error rate by factors of 3.8 in the X basis and 1.4 in the Z basis. In memory experiments of up to 150 rounds, the distance advantage weakens, alongside long-lived correlations that may reflect a persistent error component. Under our optimization recipe, increasing the protected distance from 3 to 6 while holding the other distance fixed reduces the per-round logical error rate from 0.53% to 0.24% in Z memory and from 0.52% to 0.22% in X memory. The corresponding error-suppression factors under maximum-likelihood decoding are 1.68 and 1.85. These results connect circuit compilation and optimization to surface-code memory performance and limitations, and motivate QPU and QEC circuit codesign for fault-tolerant quantum computing primitives on current cloud hardware.

infographic.key_insight: Optimized surface-code memory on a cloud-accessible IBM processor suppressed logical errors as the protected code distance increased from 3 to 6.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Readout, reset, and echo design can materially improve quantum memory performance, motivating joint optimization of QPU hardware and error-correction circuits.
method: Test rotated surface-code memories across placements on an IBM Nighthawk r2 processor.
Combine short readout, fused measurement and reset, and XX echo on data qubits during ancilla readout.
Evaluate distance scaling with maximum-likelihood decoding and memory experiments up to 150 rounds.
infographic.evidence_signal: Increasing the protected distance from 3 to 6 while holding the other distance fixed reduced per-round logical error from 0.53% to 0.24% in Z memory and from 0.52% to 0.22% in X memory.

infographic.paper_title: Demonstration of Logical Error Suppression in a Surface Code Memory on a Cloud-Accessible IBM Superconducting Processor

title: Learning angles for quantum approximate optimization
authors: Johannes Jakubik, Isabelle Wittmann, Zaheed Gaffoor, Gciniwe Simphiwe Baloyi, Craig Mahlasi, Etienne Vos
abstract: The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) and its variants are leading algorithms to help solve challenging combinatorial optimization problems. QAOA maps these problems to Ising Hamiltonians such that their ground state is the desired solution. Candidate solutions are then drawn from a variational quantum circuit. The performance of QAOA hinges on a set of variational angles. However, finding good angles is an instance-specific and computationally expensive non-convex classical optimization task. Here, we learn the mapping from the problem instance to high-quality QAOA angles. Our learned models replace the per-instance optimization, that we call the solver, with a single forward pass that is several orders of magnitude faster than the solver with a near identical quality. Our models further generalize to unseen topologies such as Barabási-Albert and 2D grid graphs. Experiments on quantum hardware confirm that QAOA samples with angles produced by our open-source models are indistinguishable from solver angles. Crucially, models sensitive to the topology of the problem instance increase the quality of the QAOA angles. Our work amortizes a major bottleneck in QAOA by an up-front data generation and training cost. Importantly, this cost can be amortized over time in settings where many similar problems are optimized on a regular basis, as is often the case in applications for industry.

infographic.key_insight: Learned models predict high-quality QAOA angles in a single forward pass, replacing costly per-instance optimization with near-identical solution quality.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Repeated optimization of similar problems could amortize model training costs while accelerating the classical angle-selection step of hybrid quantum workflows.
method: Learn a mapping from problem instances to QAOA angles.
Use topology-sensitive models to improve angle quality.
Replace per-instance angle optimization with model inference.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports inference several orders of magnitude faster than the solver, generalization to unseen Barabási–Albert and 2D grid topologies, and quantum-hardware samples indistinguishable from those using solver angles.
infographic.watch_item: Up-front data generation and training costs must be amortized, and generalization beyond the evaluated problem distributions remains uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: Learning angles for quantum approximate optimization

title: Leveraging verifiable structure in quantum circuits to find more efficient compilations with agentic AI
authors: Tanuj Khattar, Nicholas C. Rubin, Craig Gidney, Michael Broughton, Guang Hao Low, Ryan Babbush
abstract: We discuss an effective paradigm of utilizing AI agents to better compile quantum circuits when one can constrain bottleneck subroutines to have some form of classically verifiable structure. For example, when critical subroutines are composed exclusively of reversible classical logic, phasing operations, and measurement based uncomputation, one can efficiently simulate execution for classical inputs. This property facilitates efficient certification of approximate circuit synthesis via a form of fuzz testing, provided suitable assumptions on the input distribution. While this pattern was recently exploited to improve quantum cryptanalysis circuits, here we highlight the flexibility of the broader approach by discussing three important applications. (1) The computation of $1/\sqrt{x}$ that bottlenecks real space simulations of the Coulomb operator such as those important for modeling inertial confinement fusion reactors. (2) The decoding of Reed-Solomon codes which bottlenecks the decoded quantum interferometry algorithm when used to approximately solve the optimal polynomial intersection problem. And (3) the quantum look-up tables and controlled application of Givens rotations that bottleneck the most performant quantum algorithms for simulating chemistry in second quantization. We discuss reference implementations of these algorithms and how they can be constrained and verified in the interest of seeding a Kaggle competition designed to accelerate AI-based research into the optimization of their compilation.

infographic.key_insight: AI agents can search for more efficient quantum circuit compilations by exploiting subroutines whose structure enables efficient classical verification.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach targets circuit bottlenecks in Coulomb simulation, Reed–Solomon decoding, and second-quantized quantum chemistry.
method: Constrain subroutines to reversible classical logic, phasing operations, and measurement-based uncomputation.
Simulate classical inputs and use fuzz testing to check approximate circuit synthesis.
Provide reference implementations and verification constraints to seed a Kaggle optimization competition.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes three application areas and reference implementations but reports no quantitative compilation improvements or benchmark results.
infographic.watch_item: Fuzz-testing-based certification depends on assumptions about the input distribution and does not establish correctness for arbitrary quantum circuits.
infographic.paper_title: Leveraging verifiable structure in quantum circuits to find more efficient compilations with agentic AI

title: SpinControl: Control Software for Prototyping and Benchmarking of Spin-Qubit Devices and Measurement Protocols
authors: Harold B. Meerwaldt, Daniël P. van der Velde, Pieter T. Eendebak, Michiel J. Haye
abstract: Quantum computers require software to control the states of the qubits. As the actions on qubits grow in complexity with circuit execution, calibration, and benchmarking, the complexity of the control software grows in tandem. Spin-qubit quantum computers are at a stage where experimentalists need low-level access for tuning and calibration, and quantum algorithm researchers want high-level circuit-level access. In this article, we present the software design of SpinControl. SpinControl integrates three architectural metrics: 1) customizability, to allow prototyping devices and measurement protocols, is achieved by separating data and behaviour; 2) modularity and extensibility are achieved by separating functionalities into different components; and 3) robustness, to reliably execute quantum circuits on many qubits, is achieved by CI pipelines and input validation. SpinControl allows different types of measurements while customizing the instruments used, the pulse or circuit program executed, and the data processing. It allows building standardized experiments from measurement and analysis building blocks and executing these for calibration in a custom and conditional order. SpinControl implements these functionalities alongside robust configuration and data management, a connection to the cloud, and calibration scheduling. Pulse and circuit compilation, virtual gate matrices, as well as spin-qubit-specific GUIs integrated by SpinControl, make heavy use of software packages developed by Delft University of Technology: pulse lib, core-tools (both open source), and QConstruct

infographic.key_insight: SpinControl bridges low-level spin-qubit tuning and high-level circuit execution through customizable, modular control software.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It supports device prototyping, measurement protocols, calibration, and benchmarking while integrating instrument control, compilation, and data management.
method: Separate data from behavior to customize instruments, pulse or circuit programs, and processing.
Compose measurement and analysis building blocks into conditionally ordered calibration workflows.
Use modular components, CI pipelines, and input validation to support extensibility and reliable execution.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes software architecture and capabilities but reports no quantitative benchmarks or experimental performance results.
infographic.watch_item: Reliability at larger qubit counts remains unquantified in the abstract, and deployment requires integration with supporting packages and hardware.
infographic.paper_title: SpinControl: Control Software for Prototyping and Benchmarking of Spin-Qubit Devices and Measurement Protocols

title: Jianmu-Q: Bridging Quantum Field Theory and Quantum Hardware with AI Agents
authors: Xiaolin Wang, Xingyu Guo, Jinyang Li, Tianyin Li, Enke Wang, Lingxiao Wang
abstract: Quantum computing offers a promising approach to non-perturbative simulations of quantum field theories, particularly for real-time dynamics and systems affected by the sign problem. Yet translating continuum field theories into quantum computations remains a challenging interdisciplinary task. Here we introduce \texttt{Jianmu-Q}, a multi-agent framework that transforms natural-language descriptions of quantum field theories into quantum simulation workflows. Specialized agents handle theoretical formulation, lattice discretization, qubit mapping, and circuit design, while physical consistency checks and independent numerical calculations provide validation throughout the workflow. We benchmark the framework on three field theories of increasing complexity: the $(1+1)$-dimensional Nambu--Jona-Lasinio and Schwinger models, and a $(2+1)$-dimensional $\mathbb{Z}_2$ gauge theory. Across these systems, noiseless quantum-circuit simulations converge toward independent exact-diagonalization and tensor-network results, while selected circuits are executed on IBM quantum hardware, demonstrating an end-to-end, validation-guided approach to quantum simulation of field theories.

infographic.key_insight: Jianmu-Q uses specialized AI agents to translate natural-language descriptions of quantum field theories into validation-guided quantum simulation workflows.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework connects theoretical formulation to quantum-circuit design and hardware execution, addressing a key integration challenge in field-theory simulation.
method: Coordinate agents for theoretical formulation, lattice discretization, qubit mapping, and circuit design.
Validate intermediate results with physical consistency checks and independent numerical calculations.
Benchmark noiseless circuits and execute selected circuits on IBM quantum hardware.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across the (1+1)D Nambu–Jona-Lasinio and Schwinger models and a (2+1)D Z₂ gauge theory, noiseless circuit simulations converge toward independent exact-diagonalization and tensor-network results.
infographic.watch_item: Selected hardware executions demonstrate feasibility, but the abstract does not establish noise robustness, scalability, or quantum advantage.
infographic.paper_title: Jianmu-Q: Bridging Quantum Field Theory and Quantum Hardware with AI Agents

title: Expressivity of IQP Feature-Map Quantum Kernels via Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces
authors: Valeria Repetto, Stefano Melchionna, Romina D'Aurizio
abstract: Quantum kernels are among the most promising methods in quantum machine learning, providing a natural way to embed data into high-dimensional Hilbert spaces via quantum circuits and capturing non-linear relationships in data. Their learning behaviour is governed by the function class they represent, which is formally characterized by the structure of the associated Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS). However, a theoretical characterization of this function class, and of how it depends on the choice of feature map and its hyperparameters, is still lacking. In this work, we focus on the Instantaneous Quantum Polynomial (IQP) feature map and derive a Fourier representation of the associated RKHS generators as finite sums of trigonometric functions evaluated on polynomially transformed input variables, with a finite set of accessible frequencies determined by the circuit construction and scaled by the bandwidth hyperparameter. This representation identifies three bandwidth regimes with qualitatively distinct expressive properties from localised, through multimodal, to periodic. Numerical experiments on synthetic datasets with controlled periodic and multimodal structure, across data dimensions and feature-map configurations, reproduce the three regimes in both supervised classification and unsupervised anomaly detection, benchmarked against a classical Gaussian kernel. These results make the relationship between expressivity and data structure explicit for IQP kernels: expressive power translates into a practical benefit only when the accessible frequencies match with the structure of the data, which provides a criterion for selecting the bandwidth when the periodic or multimodal structure of data is known.

infographic.key_insight: IQP quantum-kernel expressivity depends on circuit-accessible frequencies and bandwidth, benefiting learning when these align with the data’s structure.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Known periodic or multimodal data structure can guide bandwidth selection rather than assuming a high-dimensional quantum embedding will improve performance.
method: Characterize the IQP kernel’s reproducing kernel Hilbert space through Fourier representations of its generators.
Express generators as finite trigonometric sums on polynomially transformed inputs, with circuit-defined frequencies scaled by bandwidth.
Identify three bandwidth regimes: localised, multimodal, and periodic.
infographic.evidence_signal: Synthetic classification and anomaly-detection experiments reproduce all three regimes across data dimensions and feature-map configurations, with a classical Gaussian kernel as the benchmark.
infographic.watch_item: Synthetic-data results do not establish general quantum advantage or robustness on noisy quantum hardware.
infographic.paper_title: Expressivity of IQP Feature-Map Quantum Kernels via Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces

title: Quantum-Assisted Unambiguous Discrimination of Pure States with Robustness Bounds
authors: Jinhyeok Heo, Dongkeun Lee, Junghee Ryu, Minjin Choi
abstract: We propose a hybrid quantum-classical framework for the unambiguous discrimination of pure states by combining the noisy intermediate-scale quantum semidefinite program solver (NSS) with the reciprocal-state representation. In NSS, a given semidefinite program (SDP) is represented within a subspace spanned by chosen ansatz states, with the required quantities estimated using quantum circuits, and the resulting optimization is performed classically. This makes NSS naturally applicable to discrimination problems involving circuit-prepared states, as finding a discrimination measurement can be formulated as an SDP. By choosing the discriminated states themselves as the ansatz and exploiting the reciprocal-state representation, the general matrix-variable NSS formulation is reduced to an optimization over N scalar variables, where N is the number of discriminated states. The resulting formulation reduces the number of optimization variables and positive-semidefinite constraints compared with the original NSS formulation. We further establish robustness guarantees against Gram matrix estimation errors, including a rescaling procedure that guarantees a valid positive operator-valued measure (POVM) under bounded perturbations. The resulting bounds quantify both the deviation in average success probability and violations of the no-error condition using only the estimated Gram matrix, its SDP solution, and a characterized perturbation bound, without access to the ideal Gram matrix. Numerical simulations validate the derived robustness bounds and characterize finite-shot scaling. We also perform experiments on IBM quantum hardware to estimate pairwise overlaps, and then evaluate the performance of the resulting POVMs.

infographic.key_insight: A hybrid quantum-classical method reduces pure-state unambiguous discrimination to an SDP with N scalar variables by combining reciprocal states with a quantum-assisted solver.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach simplifies measurement optimization for circuit-prepared states while providing computable safeguards against overlap-estimation errors.
method: Use quantum circuits to estimate the Gram matrix of the states to be discriminated.
Choose those states as the solver ansatz and use reciprocal states to reduce the classical SDP.
Bound performance degradation and rescale the solution to guarantee a valid POVM under bounded perturbations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical simulations validate robustness bounds and characterize finite-shot scaling; IBM hardware experiments estimate pairwise overlaps for subsequent POVM evaluation.
infographic.watch_item: The validity guarantee requires a characterized perturbation bound, and a valid POVM does not by itself guarantee error-free discrimination under estimation noise.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum-Assisted Unambiguous Discrimination of Pure States with Robustness Bounds

title: Agent-assisted experimental strategy transfer across quantum processors
authors: Shi-Yao Hou, Zipeng Wu, Chao Zhang, Guanru Feng, Keren Li, Jingen Xiang
abstract: Progress in quantum hardware requires a growing volume of experiments across diverse devices, straining the capacity of human experts. Automation remains challenging because device differences and drift can render workflows developed on one processor unsuitable for another. Here we present an agent-assisted experimental strategy for conducting experiments across three-qubit nuclear magnetic resonance processors. Developed on one processor and applied sequentially to four others, the strategy uses an agent to assess experimental evidence, select subsequent measurements and adapt procedures, with operators providing instrument preparation and physical intervention. Using three-qubit Grover state preparation as a common task, each deployment combined device-specific calibration, control-pulse optimization and measurement. The experimental strategy was refined through sequential deployment, and all four processors ultimately produced outputs dominated by their respective marked states. The marked-state populations of the reconstructed dominant eigenstates ranged from \(0.910\) to \(0.959\), with relative deviations below \(3.8\%\) from the ideal value of 0.945. These results demonstrate that an agent-assisted experimental strategy can be reused and refined across processors to realize a common quantum task, providing a basis for scaling experimental practice beyond individual devices.

infographic.key_insight: An agent-assisted experimental strategy was reused and refined across four additional three-qubit NMR processors to perform Grover state preparation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Evidence-driven adaptation could reduce expert workload when transferring quantum experiments between devices with different calibration and control requirements.
method: Develop the strategy on one processor, then deploy sequentially on four others.
Use an agent to assess evidence, choose measurements and adapt calibration, pulse optimization and measurement procedures.
Retain operators for instrument preparation and physical intervention.
infographic.evidence_signal: All four target processors produced marked-state-dominated outputs; marked-state populations in reconstructed dominant eigenstates ranged from 0.910 to 0.959, with relative deviations below 3.8% from the ideal 0.945.
infographic.watch_item: Results are limited to three-qubit NMR processors and one common task, with human intervention still required.
infographic.paper_title: Agent-assisted experimental strategy transfer across quantum processors

title: Solving Large-Scale Parameter Inference in Controllable Nuclear Fusion via Coherent Ising Machines and Block Coordinate Descent
authors: Zijie Liu, Wenchao Liu, Wenxin Li, Anzhe Jiang, Hongdong Zhu, Qi Gao
abstract: Bayesian inference enables self-consistent plasma parameter inversion in tokamak integrated data analysis by fusing multi-source diagnostics. However, under nonlinear Gaussian likelihoods, finding the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate typically relies on sampling methods whose high computational overhead precludes real-time plasma control. To address this bottleneck, we propose a Bayesian inversion framework using a Coherent Ising Machine (CIM)-a quantum computing architecture based on coupled degenerate optical parametric oscillators (DOPOs). With native all-to-all connectivity, the CIM directly maps the negative log-posterior potential onto a spin Hamiltonian and leverages quantum vacuum fluctuations for rapid state-space search during pitchfork bifurcation. Validated on plasma current profile inversion for the EAST tokamak, this method achieves a single-run solution time of approximately 1 ms. Although current qubit limits necessitate a block-wise iterative scheme that prevents full real-time execution today, rapidly scaling quantum hardware offers a clear pathway toward real-time tokamak control.

infographic.key_insight: A Coherent Ising Machine–based Bayesian inversion framework targets faster plasma parameter estimation for tokamak control.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Faster fusion of tokamak diagnostic data could support real-time plasma control as hardware capacity scales.
method: Formulate plasma parameter inversion as Bayesian maximum a posteriori estimation.
Map the negative log-posterior objective to a spin Hamiltonian for a coupled optical-oscillator CIM.
Use block coordinate descent to accommodate current hardware capacity limits.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation on EAST tokamak plasma current profile inversion reports an approximately 1 ms single-run solution time, not end-to-end real-time execution.
infographic.watch_item: Current hardware capacity requires block-wise iteration, which still prevents full real-time operation.
infographic.paper_title: Solving Large-Scale Parameter Inference in Controllable Nuclear Fusion via Coherent Ising Machines and Block Coordinate Descent

title: Task-aligned spectral inductive biases in parameterized quantum circuits
authors: Felix Frohnert, Adrián Pérez-Salinas, Sebastian Lange, Marcus Schwaebisch, Evert van Nieuwenburg, Vedran Dunjko
abstract: Parameterized quantum circuits are widely investigated in quantum machine learning, yet how their architecture can provide task-aligned inductive biases remains poorly understood. We study data reuploading quantum circuits with two distinct inputs: a signal that varies between samples and a fixed, task-defined spectral query that specifies how the signal should be probed. We show that encoding the query can change the circuit's hypothesis class over the signal by modulating how its existing signal frequencies are combined, without introducing new sample-dependent information. This mechanism matches tasks built on nonuniform Fourier transforms, whose evaluation frequencies specify the query and whose sampling positions guide its encoding. We examine this connection in a classification task inspired by synthetic aperture radar, where acquisition geometry determines a query for classifying unfocused spectral patches before image formation. Across small-scale spectral and radar-like tasks, aligned queries improve learning from limited data over parameter-matched circuits with mismatched or absent queries. These results provide a route from known spectral task structure to the design and validation of inductive biases in parameterized quantum circuits.

infographic.key_insight: Task-defined spectral queries steer how parameterized quantum circuits combine existing signal frequencies, creating task-aligned inductive biases without adding sample-dependent information.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Known spectral structure can guide quantum circuit design for data-limited classification, including radar-like tasks performed before image formation.
method: Use data-reuploading circuits with a sample-varying signal and a fixed, task-defined spectral query.
Align query encoding with nonuniform Fourier evaluation frequencies and sampling positions.
Compare aligned queries against parameter-matched circuits with mismatched or absent queries.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across small-scale spectral and synthetic-aperture-radar-inspired classification tasks, aligned queries improved learning from limited data over parameter-matched baselines.
infographic.watch_item: Small-scale results do not establish scalability, robustness on noisy quantum hardware, or advantage over classical methods.
infographic.paper_title: Task-aligned spectral inductive biases in parameterized quantum circuits

title: ConQUESTA: Topology-Aware Post-Training Structural Pruning of Quantum Neural Networks
authors: Saim Rehman, Muhammad Shafique
abstract: Deploying quantum neural networks (QNNs) on sparse hardware requires preserving task accuracy while reducing compiler-induced two-qubit gates, SWAPs, and depth. We present ConQUESTA (\underline{C}onstrained \underline{Qu}antum \underline{E}ntangler \underline{S}election with \underline{T}opology \underline{A}wareness), a post training pruning framework that combines task saliency with compiler cost, screens candidate entanglers, and searches complete pruning masks under an explicit accuracy constraint. Unlike one-shot ranking, each mask is transpiled as a whole across multiple coupling topologies. Across 4-, 6-, and 8-qubit QNNs and eight model seeds at 55% pruning, ConQUESTA achieves mean resource reductions of 61.6% on Breast Cancer, 72.0% on Digits01, and 82.2% on Iris, exceeding the strongest matched simple baseline by 3.5, 1.7, and 8.9 percentage points, respectively. Fixed-mask recovery raises feasibility from 16/24 to 22/24 runs. In a fixed-k=4 scaling study on a scaling probe of 4 to 12-qubits, the raw mask space grew from 495 to 12.1M while the evaluated masks increase only from 189 to 305. Resource-weight changes alter depth/routing priorities with at most a 0.44-point mean validation shift.

infographic.key_insight: ConQUESTA prunes quantum neural network entanglers using task saliency and hardware-topology-aware compilation costs to reduce resources under an explicit accuracy constraint.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework targets sparse quantum hardware, where pruning must account for compiler-induced two-qubit gates, SWAPs, and circuit depth.
method: Screen candidate entanglers using task saliency and compiler cost.
Search complete pruning masks, transpiling each across multiple coupling topologies.
Apply fixed-mask recovery to improve accuracy-constraint feasibility.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 4-, 6-, and 8-qubit QNNs with eight model seeds at 55% pruning, mean resource reductions were 61.6%–82.2% across three datasets, exceeding the strongest matched simple baseline by 1.7–8.9 percentage points.
infographic.watch_item: Recovery improved feasibility to 22/24 runs, but accuracy constraints were not always met; scaling evidence extends only to a 12-qubit probe.
infographic.paper_title: ConQUESTA: Topology-Aware Post-Training Structural Pruning of Quantum Neural Networks

title: Programmable Preparation of Topological Entangled States
authors: M. Javad Zakeri, Alaric Pan, Darren D Hudson, Andrea Blanco-Redondo
abstract: Programmable preparation of entangled quantum states is a central requirement for scalable quantum information processing, quantum networking and photonic quantum computing. Topological photonic platforms offer an attractive route towards robust quantum-state generation by encoding information in symmetry- protected optical modes, yet the generated entangled states are typically dictated by the lattice geometry and therefore lack programmability. Here we demonstrate programmable preparation of topological entangled states by inverse engineering the nonlinear optical pump profile of an integrated photonic lattice. Our approach enables deterministic control over both the dimensionality and modal structure of the generated entangled state while preserving its topological character. We experimentally realize silicon photonic topological superlattices in which the nonlinear generation pathway itself becomes programmable via tailored excitations. The superlattices host a multiband manifold of co localized topological interface modes, while coherently controlled inputs synthesize pump superpositions within this protected basis. We showcase this principle by selectively addressing topological biphoton eigenstates, steering correlations to produce a desired target state in a high-dimensional Hilbert space, and inverse-designing pump states that generate targeted Schmidt dimensionalities. Site-resolved two-photon correlation measurements remain reproducible across nominally identical fabricated devices, demonstrating robustness to realistic nanofabrication-induced disorder. Programmable preparation of topological entangled states establishes a pathway towards exploiting topological photonic modes as application-specific quantum resources, enabling tailored input states for high-dimensional quantum communication, quantum networking and photonic quantum computing.

infographic.key_insight: Tailoring the optical pump makes topological photonic entangled states programmable in dimensionality and modal structure while preserving their topological character.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Programmable silicon photonic sources could supply application-specific entangled states for high-dimensional quantum communication, networking and photonic quantum computing.
method: Fabricate silicon photonic superlattices supporting co-localized topological interface modes.
Inverse-engineer nonlinear pump profiles using coherent input superpositions.
Target biphoton eigenstates, spatial correlations and Schmidt dimensionalities.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments demonstrate targeted state preparation, with site-resolved two-photon correlations reproducible across nominally identical devices despite fabrication-induced disorder.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify state fidelity, generation efficiency or scalability, leaving practical system performance uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: Programmable Preparation of Topological Entangled States

title: Circuit Synthesis for Variational Quantum Algorithms: The Depth of Algebra and Geometry
authors: Boris Tsvelikhovskiy
abstract: The analysis of Hamiltonian Variational Ansätze centers on three fundamental questions: which states are exactly reachable from a given initial state, what native control depth suffices for local and global synthesis, and whether a bounded circuit extension can expose a direction of decreasing cost at a suboptimal output. We address these challenges by leveraging the dynamical Lie algebras (DLAs) associated with the circuits and the geometry of the initial state's orbit under the action of the corresponding dynamical Lie group $G$. We show that an initial state has a closed projective orbit whenever it is a nondegenerate eigenstate of a control Hamiltonian. Combined with asymptotic QAOA convergence, this guarantees exact, finite depth ground state preparation for architectures employing diagonal problem Hamiltonians and irreducible stoquastic mixers. We bound the number of native control exponentials required for local unitary synthesis and state preparation using DLA commutator filtration growth alongside reachable orbit dimensions. Complementing these local results, we construct global frameworks on invariant sectors equipped with full unitary or special unitary dynamical Lie algebras. These constructions yield explicit applications to Pauli-generated systems and constrained maximum independent set multi-angle QAOA circuits; specifically, we show that their native control costs are directly determined by commutator filtration depth and independent-set toggle-group geometry, respectively. Finally, if the dynamical Lie group is compact, the observable $H_P$ generates an admissible evolution ($iH_P \in \mathfrak{g}$, where $\mathfrak{g}$ is the DLA), and the projective orbit of the initial state contains a ground state ray of $H_P$, then a bounded depth, identity-initialized circuit extension exhibits either first-order descent or negative curvature at every suboptimal circuit output.

infographic.key_insight: Dynamical Lie algebras and reachable-state geometry characterize exact state preparation, bound native circuit depth, and identify bounded circuit extensions that enable descent from suboptimal outputs under stated conditions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results provide architecture-specific guidance for variational circuit synthesis, linking native control costs to algebraic structure and reachable-state geometry.
method: Analyze dynamical Lie groups and projective orbits to establish exact reachability.
Use commutator filtration growth and orbit dimensions to bound local synthesis costs.
Construct global synthesis frameworks and bounded-depth extensions that expose descent directions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical guarantees and applications to Pauli-generated systems and constrained maximum independent set multi-angle QAOA, but no numerical or hardware benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Guarantees depend on structural assumptions such as compactness, admissible cost evolution, and ground-state reachability; finite depth alone does not establish hardware-efficient execution.
infographic.paper_title: Circuit Synthesis for Variational Quantum Algorithms: The Depth of Algebra and Geometry

title: Energetics of Fault-Tolerant Spin-Qubit Quantum Computation
authors: João Santos, Jayshankar Nath, Marco Pezzutto, Valentin Savin, Tristan Meunier, Yasser Omar
abstract: Semiconductor spin qubits offer a promising route to compact and scalable quantum computers, combining long coherence times in isotopically purified silicon with compatibility with semiconductor manufacturing. Beyond computational speedup, their energy efficiency is an important consideration for future large-scale systems. We evaluate the power and energy requirements of a Loss-DiVincenzo spin-qubit quantum computer by analyzing the Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT) and benchmarking it against the classical Fast Fourier Transform (FFT). We develop a detailed energy budget, identifying cryogenic cooling as the dominant baseline contribution before quantum error correction (QEC). The comparison between the QFT and the classical FFT reveals that, for any quantum workload operating under a polynomially bounded sampling regime, the crossover in energy consumption occurs at smaller problem sizes than the crossover in execution time. Thus, quantum computing can become energetically competitive before achieving a speedup in execution time. We then incorporate surface-code QEC and analyze the energy costs of QEC cycles, gate synthesis, and decoding. At scale, instrumentation and decoding become dominant contributions, while cryogenic cooling imposes a constraint on scalability. We show that optimizing the control-signal demultiplexing ratio can reduce the overall energy cost by approximately two orders of magnitude. For a system with about one million physical qubits, we estimate a power consumption of approximately 100 kW, at least one order of magnitude below that of today's highest-performance classical computing systems.

infographic.key_insight: Spin-qubit quantum computers could become energy-competitive with classical computing before achieving an execution-time advantage.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Optimizing control-signal demultiplexing could reduce fault-tolerant system energy costs by approximately 100×, making control architecture a critical design choice.
method: Model the energy budget of a Loss–DiVincenzo spin-qubit quantum computer.
Compare quantum Fourier transform energy and runtime against classical FFT under polynomially bounded sampling.
Include surface-code error correction, gate synthesis, and decoding costs.
infographic.evidence_signal: The model estimates approximately 100 kW for one million physical qubits, at least 10× below today's highest-performance classical computing systems.
infographic.watch_item: These are model-based estimates; instrumentation and decoding dominate at scale, while cryogenic cooling constrains scalability.
infographic.paper_title: Energetics of Fault-Tolerant Spin-Qubit Quantum Computation

title: Connectivity Bounds for GHZ Graphs
authors: L. Sunil Chandran, Rishikesh Gajjala
abstract: Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) states are multipartite entangled quantum states that play a central role in quantum information theory, with applications in quantum communication, cryptography, and distributed quantum computing. A major experimental goal is to create high-dimensional GHZ states using multiple entangled parties. Krenn, Gu and Zeilinger discovered a surprising bridge between these quantum-optical experiments and graph theory: certain photonic experiments can be represented by edge-coloured, edge-weighted graphs, and the dimension of the produced GHZ state equals the number of feasible monochromatic inherited vertex colourings. This led Krenn and Gu to conjecture that every GHZ graph with more than four vertices has dimension at most $2$. A counterexample would give a new high-dimensional multipartite GHZ construction, while a proof would clarify fundamental resource limitations in quantum optics. It is known that the conjecture holds for graphs of vertex connectivity at most $2$ [MFCS 2024], and that simple GHZ graphs with $n>4$ vertices have dimension less than $n/\sqrt{2}$ [Quantum 2024]. However, no general upper bound depending only on vertex connectivity was known. We prove that every simple connected GHZ graph $G$ with at least four vertices has dimension at most $2^{κ(G)-1}+\binom{κ(G)}{2}$, where $κ(G)$ is the vertex connectivity of $G$. We also prove new bounds in terms of edge connectivity and maximum degree.

infographic.key_insight: Every simple connected GHZ graph with at least four vertices has dimension at most 2^(κ(G)−1) + κ(G)(κ(G)−1)/2, where κ(G) is vertex connectivity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The bound links graph connectivity to achievable GHZ-state dimension, providing a theoretical constraint for graph-based photonic entanglement designs.
method: Use the graph representation of photonic experiments, where feasible monochromatic inherited vertex colourings determine GHZ dimension.
Prove an upper bound depending only on vertex connectivity.
Derive additional bounds involving edge connectivity and maximum degree.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports mathematical proofs, not experimental measurements or numerical benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: The result applies to simple connected GHZ graphs and does not resolve the general conjecture that dimension is at most 2 for graphs with more than four vertices.
infographic.paper_title: Connectivity Bounds for GHZ Graphs

title: Same Spectrum, Harder First-Order Training: Phase-Locking in Single- versus Multi-Qubit Re-Uploading Circuits
authors: Michael Poppel, David Bucher, Maximilian Zorn, Markus Baumann, Sebastian Wölckert, Claudia Linnhoff-Popien
abstract: Angle-encoded variational quantum circuits implement truncated Fourier series. For one-dimensional inputs, a single-qubit re-uploading (serial) circuit represents every function that a multi-qubit circuit with the same encoding budget $E$ can; we find that this exchange of width for depth is not free in first-order training. Because its state lives on the Bloch sphere, all parameters of the serial circuit move the state, at each input, along one complex direction, which we call \emph{phase-locking}. We prove that this costs no Fourier direction but leaves no direction to spare: however many parameters it has, the serial circuit has at most $2E+2$ tangent directions, one more than its $2E+1$ Fourier coefficients need, while a two-qubit control with the same encoding budget and model class generically has at least $6E+6$. The cost in training is measured against this control, as the number of runs out of 100 that reach the optimum within a fixed step budget. On an exact loss with flat-spectrum targets the gap grows with $E$; at $E=32$ the serial circuit converges in 3, 53 and 83 runs under gradient descent, Adam and Levenberg--Marquardt, the control in 99, 100 and 100. On three real-world series, at matched parameter counts, the serial circuit reaches the least-squares optimum in at most 9 runs under Adam and in 32 to 93 under Levenberg--Marquardt, the control in at least 98 and in all 100; its held-out error is up to about $1.5$ times that of the control under Adam, but no larger in the typical run under Levenberg--Marquardt.

infographic.key_insight: Single-qubit re-uploading circuits can match multi-qubit Fourier expressivity at the same encoding budget, yet phase-locking makes first-order training substantially harder.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Trading qubit width for circuit depth can preserve representational power while reducing optimization reliability under a fixed training budget.
method: Compare serial single-qubit circuits with two-qubit controls at matched encoding budgets and model classes.
Prove a serial tangent-direction ceiling of 2E+2, versus generically at least 6E+6 for the two-qubit control.
Evaluate gradient descent, Adam and Levenberg–Marquardt on exact flat-spectrum losses and three real-world series.
infographic.evidence_signal: At E=32, serial circuits reached the optimum in 3/53/83 of 100 runs under gradient descent/Adam/Levenberg–Marquardt, versus 99/100/100 for the control; real-series tests also favored the control's convergence.
infographic.watch_item: Results concern one-dimensional inputs and specific circuit comparisons; convergence gaps should not be generalized to all quantum models or interpreted as demonstrated hardware advantages.
infographic.paper_title: Same Spectrum, Harder First-Order Training: Phase-Locking in Single- versus Multi-Qubit Re-Uploading Circuits

title: Magic in quantum trajectory unravelings of noisy random quantum circuits
authors: Sara Santos, Alessio Paviglianiti, Vincenzo Savona
abstract: The quantum-trajectory description of a noisy quantum circuit is not unique: every Kraus representation of the noise channel defines a different unraveling, i.e., a different ensemble of pure states that averages to the same density matrix. While all unravelings share the same expectation values of observables, they generally differ in the amount of quantum resources carried by the individual trajectories. Here we study non-stabilizerness, or magic, quantified by the stabilizer Rényi entropy, in quantum-trajectory unravelings of Haar-random and $T$-doped random Clifford brickwork circuits subject to local dephasing noise of strength $p$. The canonical unraveling in terms of Pauli jumps is Clifford and leaves magic untouched, so that trajectories retain the Haar-random value of non-stabilizerness. Exploring the full two-parameter family of minimal unravelings, we find that the trajectory-averaged magic can be substantially reduced by a state-independent choice of Kraus operators, and that the optimal choice is not in general the projective-measurement unraveling, but a two-outcome generalized measurement in which the Kraus operators correspond to a weak measurement of the noisy qubit. The optimal unraveling reduces the extensive magic density of the trajectories by a $p$-dependent factor without altering its linear scaling with system size. At the same time, it produces a very broad distribution of magic over trajectories, with a sizable fraction of trajectories retaining Haar-random magic. Since the cost of stabilizer-based classical simulation grows exponentially with the magic of the state, these high-magic trajectories, rather than the average, control the simulation cost. Our results delineate the potential and the limitations of unraveling optimization as a route to the classical simulation of noisy quantum dynamics with stabilizer methods.

infographic.key_insight: Choosing a weak-measurement unraveling can substantially reduce average trajectory magic without changing the noisy circuit’s density matrix, but high-magic trajectories persist.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Unraveling optimization may lower typical stabilizer-based simulation costs, but average magic alone is insufficient to predict computational savings.
method: Study locally dephased Haar-random and T-doped random Clifford brickwork circuits.
Quantify trajectory magic using stabilizer Rényi entropy.
Explore a two-parameter family of minimal Kraus unravelings with state-independent choices.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a noise-dependent reduction in magic density, while magic remains linear in system size and its trajectory distribution remains broad.
infographic.watch_item: A sizable fraction of trajectories retains Haar-random magic and can dominate simulation cost because stabilizer-based costs grow exponentially with magic.
infographic.paper_title: Magic in quantum trajectory unravelings of noisy random quantum circuits

title: Concrete Functions in Private Simultaneous Quantum Messages: Quantum Advantages and Structural Limitations
authors: Harumichi Nishimura
abstract: Private simultaneous quantum messages (PSQM) provide a minimal model of noninteractive secure multiparty quantum computation, yet their communication complexity for concrete functions remains poorly understood. We show that familiar total functions already exhibit both genuine quantum advantages and strong structural limitations. For three-party equality on $n$-bit inputs, which determines whether the players' $n$-bit strings are identical, we construct an entanglement-assisted protocol with asymptotic communication $(1.633\ldots)n$ qubits, whereas every perfectly correct protocol without prior entanglement requires at least $3n$ qubits. For three-bit majority, one shared GHZ state and one transmitted qubit per player suffice for perfect correctness and perfect privacy, reducing the communication from the optimal classical cost of six bits to three qubits. Three-bit AND behaves differently. No perfectly correct and perfectly private protocol exists when the players share an arbitrary three-qubit state, apply arbitrary local unitary encodings, and transmit one qubit each. However, increasing the local dimension overcomes this obstruction: one shared three-qutrit GHZ state and one transmitted qutrit per player yield a one-shot protocol with total communication $3\log_2 3$. Together with the six-bit classical lower bound, this gives a strict quantum communication advantage. More generally, for every $k\geq 3$, we construct a perfectly correct and perfectly private one-shot protocol for $k$-bit AND using one qudit of dimension at most $k$ per player, and hence at most $k\log_2 k$ qubits in total.

infographic.key_insight: Entanglement enables perfectly private quantum communication advantages for concrete functions, but three-bit AND requires more than one qubit per player within the studied encoding model.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These results identify communication savings and local-dimension requirements for designing noninteractive secure multiparty quantum protocols.
method: Construct entanglement-assisted protocols for three-party equality and three-bit majority.
Prove a three-bit AND impossibility for shared three-qubit states with local unitary encodings.
Construct GHZ-based qutrit and higher-dimensional qudit protocols for AND.
infographic.evidence_signal: Theoretical constructions and lower bounds show equality costs asymptotically 1.633…n qubits versus at least 3n without entanglement, majority costs 3 qubits versus 6 classical bits, and three-bit AND costs 3 log₂ 3 qubits versus 6 classical bits.
infographic.watch_item: The AND impossibility is restricted to the stated three-qubit local-unitary model; hardware noise and entanglement-distribution costs are not evaluated in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Concrete Functions in Private Simultaneous Quantum Messages: Quantum Advantages and Structural Limitations
